meta.location: The land of Gideon, written to Moroni's camp
principles: The conditions under which blood may be shed

world_behind.title: This is the answer to Alma 60
world_behind.text: Verse 1 says the reply came soon after Moroni sent his letter. The accusation of treason stood for one chapter of the record.

world_behind.title: Pahoran is writing from exile
world_behind.text: Verse 5 says he was driven out and fled to the land of Gideon with as many men as he could get. Moroni had addressed the letter to him "in the city of Zarahemla."

world_behind.title: Zarahemla is held by a king
world_behind.text: Verse 8 says the rebels took the city, appointed a king, and made an alliance with the king of the Lamanites to hold it.

world_behind.title: The withheld provisions are accounted for
world_behind.text: Verse 4 says the rebels withheld them and frightened the freemen out of marching. Helaman had reported the shortage in Alma 58:34.

world_behind.title: Pahoran had raised a force before the letter arrived
world_behind.text: Verse 6 says he sent a proclamation and men were flocking to him daily.

world_behind.title: He was already weighing the same question
world_behind.text: Verse 19 says he was worried about whether attacking his own countrymen would be just, and verse 20 takes Moroni's report of a commandment as the answer.

world_behind.title: Lehi and Teancum are named as the eastern command
world_behind.text: Verse 15 has Pahoran directing that they be given power to conduct the war while Moroni marches inland.

words.text: Intimidated into inaction. The word occurs once in the record and never in the King James Bible. Pahoran uses it of freemen who were willing to march and were frightened out of it.

An open refusal to yield, or the state of being held at bay. The record uses it three times, at Alma 5:18, 3 Nephi 6:30, and here. Pahoran applies it to the rebels, who now decline to come out and fight.
A formal league between powers. Both of the record's uses fall in this one verse, of the compact between the king in Zarahemla and the king of the Lamanites.
Formally blamed or rebuked. The word occurs once in scripture, here, where Pahoran names what Moroni's letter did to him and sets it aside in the same sentence.
Treated at Alma 41:2, of what justice demands. Pahoran uses it for the one condition under which he would accept bondage, and verse 13 says God has given no such command.
Treated at Alma 46:16, where Moroni prays against them. Pahoran groups them with rebellions as the evil that words cannot resist.

phrases.term: I do not joy in your great afflictions, yea, it grieves my soul
phrases.text: Pahoran's first sentence after identifying himself. He answers the charge of indifference by naming his own grief before giving any facts.

phrases.term: There are those who do joy in your afflictions
phrases.text: The correction, made without contradicting Moroni directly. Pahoran grants that someone was glad of the suffering and identifies who.

phrases.term: They have used great flattery, and they have led away the hearts of many people
phrases.text: The method of the rebellion. Mormon reported the same method of Amalickiah in Alma 46 and 47, and of the king-men in Alma 51.
The answer to the question Helaman and Moroni both asked. Neither commander had a way to learn it from where they stood.

phrases.term: I have fled to the land of Gideon
phrases.text: The governor of the land is a refugee. Moroni had addressed his letter to Zarahemla, where Pahoran no longer was.

phrases.term: They have appointed a king over them
phrases.text: The king-men program of Alma 51 carried out. Mosiah 29:21 warned what removing such a king would cost.

phrases.term: In your epistle you have censured me, but it mattereth not
phrases.text: The most quoted line of the chapter. Pahoran takes the accusation of treason, sets it down, and moves to the plan.

phrases.term: I am not angry, but do rejoice in the greatness of your heart
phrases.text: His reading of the letter that accused him. He treats the ferocity as evidence of what Moroni cares about.

phrases.term: We would subject ourselves to the yoke of bondage if it were requisite with the justice of God
phrases.text: The condition Pahoran places above his own liberty. Verse 13 says God has commanded trust in him instead.

phrases.term: Whatsoever evil we cannot resist with our words... let us resist them with our swords
phrases.text: The rule Pahoran states for civil war. Words first, and the sword only where words have no purchase, against rebellion and dissension.

phrases.term: I was somewhat worried concerning what we should do
phrases.text: Pahoran had been stalled by a scruple about attacking his own people. Verse 20 says Moroni's report of a commandment resolved it.

verses.label: v. 2
verses.title: A reply that names both offices before anything else
verses.text: The record opens the second letter with a formula the first did not use: "I, Pahoran, who am the chief governor of this land, do send these words unto Moroni, the chief captain over the army." Both men are identified by title, and the titles mark the constitutional relation the previous chapter's ultimatum had put in question. Alma 60:1 introduced its letter with no such formula, so the reply supplies a frame the accusation lacked.

verses.label: v. 3–5
verses.title: The missing facts, delivered without reproach
verses.text: The information Moroni did not have is given in three verses and in plain order: "there are those who do joy in your afflictions, yea, insomuch that they have risen up in rebellion against me"; "it is those who have sought to take away the judgment-seat from me that have been the cause of this great iniquity"; "they have driven me out before them, and I have fled to the land of Gideon." No sentence in the passage points out that the accusation was mistaken. The correction is made entirely by supplying what was not known.

verses.label: v. 9
verses.title: A censure dismissed in eleven words
verses.text: The response to a letter that threatened insurrection is one clause of forgiveness and one of praise: "in your epistle you have censured me, but it mattereth not; I am not angry, but do rejoice in the greatness of your heart." It mattereth not stands in eleven verses of the volume, and Moroni's own letters use it too, at Alma 58:37. The reply neither denies the charge nor accepts it. It sets the question aside and moves to the campaign.

verses.label: v. 10–13
verses.title: Pacifism stated three times, and then bounded
verses.text: The record gives three conditional refusals in a row: "We would not shed the blood of the Lamanites if they would stay in their own land"; "We would not shed the blood of our brethren if they would not rise up in rebellion and take the sword against us"; "We would subject ourselves to the yoke of bondage if it were requisite with the justice of God." Each one names the condition under which peace would hold. Verse 13 supplies the limit that overrides all three: "behold he doth not command us that we shall subject ourselves to our enemies, but that we should put our trust in him."

verses.label: v. 15–18
verses.title: The civil authority issues military orders
verses.text: The letter turns operational and the instructions are specific: "come unto me speedily with a few of your men, and leave the remainder in the charge of Lehi and Teancum; give unto them power to conduct the war in that part of the land." Verse 17 adds a mobilisation order, "Gather together whatsoever force ye can upon your march hither," and verse 18 states the objective and its purpose, "we will take possession of the city of Zarahemla, that we may obtain more food to send forth unto Lehi and Teancum." The governor is directing the general's dispositions, and the chapter reports it as ordinary.

verses.label: v. 19–20
verses.title: The accusing letter is credited with settling a doubt
verses.text: The record supplies a reason for the joy that the reader would not guess: "I do joy in receiving your epistle, for I was somewhat worried concerning what we should do, whether it should be just in us to go against our brethren." Verse 20 identifies which sentence resolved it: "ye have said, except they repent the Lord hath commanded you that ye should go against them." A letter written to shame a man is reported as having answered a question he was already asking.

verses.label: v. 21
verses.title: A closing instruction that is not military
verses.text: The last verse turns from the campaign to two named officers and their morale: "See that ye strengthen Lehi and Teancum in the Lord; tell them to fear not, for God will deliver them, yea, and also all those who stand fast in that liberty wherewith God hath made them free." The phrase at the end is the one Helaman used of the young men at Alma 58:40, and it matches Gal. 5:1. The letter ends by asking a general to carry a message of reassurance rather than an order.

chapter.title: The accusation is answered with information
chapter.text: Pahoran corrects the facts of Alma 60 in four verses and never disputes the tone.

chapter.title: The silence had a cause nobody at the front could see
chapter.text: The provisions were withheld by rebels, and the freemen were frightened into staying home. Helaman guessed at a faction in Alma 58:36 and was right.

chapter.title: The king-men finally got their king
chapter.text: Verse 8 completes what Alma 51:5 described as their aim, and the price is an alliance with the Lamanite king that would end in conquest.

chapter.title: Pahoran's reply becomes the standard for taking correction
chapter.text: Verse 9 sets the censure aside, refuses anger, and reads the letter as evidence of Moroni's heart.

chapter.title: He states limits on his own cause
chapter.text: Verses 10 through 12 name what would stop him: Lamanites who stayed home, brethren who put down the sword, or a command from God to accept bondage.

chapter.title: Words come before swords
chapter.text: Verse 14 puts the sword where speech has failed, and names rebellion and dissension as the cases.

chapter.title: Each man needed the other
chapter.text: Moroni needed the facts; Pahoran needed a warrant to move against his own people. Verses 19 and 20 say the letter supplied it.

chapter.title: The letter ends where Moroni's began
chapter.text: Verse 21 has Pahoran telling Lehi and Teancum to fear not, and blessing all who stand fast in the liberty wherewith God made them free.

applications.title: Start with the other person's trouble
applications.text: Pahoran's first sentence after his own name says that Moroni's afflictions grieve his soul. Before you set out your side of it, say that you have registered theirs.

applications.title: Answer the facts and skip the tone
applications.text: Pahoran corrected what Moroni had wrong and never mentioned how it was said. When an accusation is loud and mistaken, the correction is the useful part.

applications.title: Read who your opponents have reached out to
applications.text: The rebels held Zarahemla, set up a king, and wrote to the king of the Lamanites to make an alliance. When an internal faction goes outside for support, the dispute has changed shape and your answer to it has to change as well.

applications.title: Read anger for what it is about
applications.text: Pahoran took Moroni's ferocity as evidence that he cared about the country. Ask what someone is defending before deciding what they are attacking.

applications.title: Name what would change your mind
applications.text: Pahoran stated the conditions under which he would stop fighting or accept bondage. Knowing your own limits keeps a cause from becoming an appetite.

applications.title: Leave the rest in named hands
applications.text: Pahoran asked Moroni to come with a few men and give Lehi and Teancum power to conduct the war in that quarter. When you pull someone away for an emergency, say who now holds what they were carrying and what authority comes with it.

applications.title: Say when you were stuck
applications.text: Pahoran admitted he had been worried and unable to act. Telling someone their message unstuck you is worth more than agreement.

applications.title: Pass the encouragement down the line
applications.text: Pahoran's closing instruction was to strengthen Lehi and Teancum and tell them to fear not. Encouragement handed to a leader is meant to travel, so finish by naming who else needs to hear it.

questions.text: Who benefits from a difficulty I have blamed on someone else?
What did I not know that would have changed my judgment?
When was I last censured unfairly, and what did I do with it?
Whose harshness could I read as evidence of what they care about?
What would I give up if God required it?
What am I trying to resist with words that words cannot reach?
What decision am I stalled on for want of a warrant?

entries.head: Alma 60:1

anchor.quote: I, Pahoran, who am the chief governor of this land

entries.reason: the letter this one answers, addressed to him at Zarahemla

targets.quote: I direct mine epistle to Pahoran, in the city of Zarahemla,
targets.verse_text: And it came to pass that he wrote again to the governor of the land, who was Pahoran, and these are the words which he wrote, saying: Behold, I direct mine epistle to Pahoran, in the city of Zarahemla, who is the chief judge and the governor over the land, and also to all those who have been chosen by this people to govern and manage the affairs of this war.
targets.markdown: And it came to pass that he wrote again to the governor of the land, who was Pahoran, and these are the words which he wrote, saying: Behold, **I direct mine epistle to Pahoran, in the city of Zarahemla**, who is the chief judge and the governor over the land, and also to all those who have been chosen by this people to govern and manage the affairs of this war.

entries.head: Alma 58:36

anchor.quote: those who have sought to take away the judgment-seat from me

entries.reason: Helaman naming a faction in the government as his fear

targets.quote: we fear that there is some faction in the government,
targets.verse_text: And if it is not so, behold, we fear that there is some faction in the government, that they do not send more men to our assistance; for we know that they are more numerous than that which they have sent.
targets.markdown: And if it is not so, behold, **we fear that there is some faction in the government**, that they do not send more men to our assistance; for we know that they are more numerous than that which they have sent.

entries.head: Alma 58:34
entries.reason: the question Helaman could not answer from the field

targets.quote: we do not know the cause that the government does not grant us more strength;
targets.verse_text: Now we do not know the cause that the government does not grant us more strength; neither do those men who came up unto us know why we have not received greater strength.
targets.markdown: Now **we do not know the cause that the government does not grant us more strength**; neither do those men who came up unto us know why we have not received greater strength.

entries.head: Alma 51:5

anchor.quote: they have appointed a king over them

entries.reason: the king-men aim stated, years before it succeeded

targets.quote: to overthrow the free government and to establish a king over the land.
targets.verse_text: And it came to pass that those who were desirous that Pahoran should be dethroned from the judgment-seat were called king-men, for they were desirous that the law should be altered in a manner to overthrow the free government and to establish a king over the land.
targets.markdown: And it came to pass that those who were desirous that Pahoran should be dethroned from the judgment-seat were called king-men, for they were desirous that the law should be altered in a manner **to overthrow the free government and to establish a king over the land**.

entries.head: Alma 60:36

anchor.quote: I, Pahoran, do not seek for power, save only to retain my judgment-seat

entries.reason: Moroni disclaiming ambition in nearly the same words

targets.quote: I seek not for power, but to pull it down.
targets.verse_text: Behold, I am Moroni, your chief captain. I seek not for power, but to pull it down. I seek not for honor of the world, but for the glory of my God, and the freedom and welfare of my country. And thus I close mine epistle.
targets.markdown: Behold, I am Moroni, your chief captain. **I seek not for power, but to pull it down**. I seek not for honor of the world, but for the glory of my God, and the freedom and welfare of my country. And thus I close mine epistle.

entries.head: Alma 60:18

anchor.quote: in your epistle you have censured me, but it mattereth not

entries.reason: the sentence that censured him, admitting his ignorance

targets.quote: We know not but what ye are also traitors to your country.
targets.verse_text: But why should I say much concerning this matter? For we know not but what ye yourselves are seeking for authority. We know not but what ye are also traitors to your country.
targets.markdown: But why should I say much concerning this matter? For we know not but what ye yourselves are seeking for authority. **We know not but what ye are also traitors to your country**.

entries.head: Alma 43:47

anchor.quote: we will resist wickedness even unto bloodshed

entries.reason: the rule the fathers were given about defending themselves

targets.quote: Ye shall defend your families even unto bloodshed.
targets.verse_text: And again, the Lord has said that: Ye shall defend your families even unto bloodshed. Therefore for this cause were the Nephites contending with the Lamanites, to defend themselves, and their families, and their lands, their country, and their rights, and their religion.
targets.markdown: And again, the Lord has said that: **Ye shall defend your families even unto bloodshed**. Therefore for this cause were the Nephites contending with the Lamanites, to defend themselves, and their families, and their lands, their country, and their rights, and their religion.

entries.head: Mosiah 29:21

anchor.quote: they have appointed a king over them

entries.reason: Mosiah naming the cost of removing a seated king

targets.quote: ye cannot dethrone an iniquitous king save it be through much contention,

targets.markdown: And behold, now I say unto you, **ye cannot dethrone an iniquitous king save it be through much contention**, and the shedding of much blood.

entries.head: Mosiah 29:32

anchor.quote: that I may preserve the rights and the liberty of my people

entries.reason: the purpose Mosiah gave for the reign of judges

targets.quote: every man may enjoy his rights and privileges alike,
targets.verse_text: And now I desire that this inequality should be no more in this land, especially among this my people; but I desire that this land be a land of liberty, and every man may enjoy his rights and privileges alike, so long as the Lord sees fit that we may live and inherit the land, yea, even as long as any of our posterity remains upon the face of the land.
targets.markdown: And now I desire that this inequality should be no more in this land, especially among this my people; but I desire that this land be a land of liberty, and **every man may enjoy his rights and privileges alike**, so long as the Lord sees fit that we may live and inherit the land, yea, even as long as any of our posterity remains upon the face of the land.
